paper_title: CompactSplat: Spatially Adaptive Gaussian Distribution for Feedforward Scene Reconstruction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse views without per-scene optimization remains highly challenging, especially for recovering accurate geometry and fine textures. While recent feedforward approaches leverage generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for scene generation, they typically assign one or multiple Gaussians to each pixel. Such uniform allocation not only produces highly redundant representations by wasting primitives in homogeneous areas, but also fails to exploit the inherent geometric priors of planar surfaces, often resulting in sub-optimal structural modeling. To address these limitations, we present CompactSplat, a novel feedforward framework that enables a content-aware allocation of 3D Gaussians. By integrating texture-guided spatial partitioning with hierarchical sampling, CompactSplat adaptively distributes primitives - concentrating dense Gaussians in complex regions while tiling flat areas with expanded, scale-modulated primitives. Moreover, our framework inherently supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time, enabling seamless trade-offs between rendering fidelity and memory footprint without requiring network retraining. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, DL3DV, and ScanNet demonstrate that CompactSplat consistently outperforms prior methods on both standard metrics and high-resolution rendering consistency, achieving high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly fewer primitives.

While previous methods typically allocate one or more Gaussians per pixelleading to excessive primitives and spatially redundant representations, CompactSplat adaptively allocates primitives based on regional complexity. It concentrates dense Gaussians in texturally rich areas while deploying expanded, scale-modulated primitives in flat regions. This paradigm enables high-fidelity reconstruction with substantially fewer primitives. Crucially, it inherently supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time, allowing seamless trade-offs between visual fidelity and memory footprint across diverse deployment constraints.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recovering geometrically accurate and visually consistent 3D scenes from sparse views is fundamental problem for immersive VR, gaming, and digital content creation. The recent success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Kerbl et al. (2023) has significantly advanced this field by representing scenes as collections of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time rendering with high visual fidelity. Existing methods for constructing such representations generally follow two paradigms. Traditional approaches rely on dense multi-view captures and COLMAP-based Schönberger and Frahm (2016) point cloud initialization, followed by computationally expensive per-scene optimization. To avoid this bottleneck, feed-forward approaches have recently gained increasing attention. By leveraging pretrained models, they directly predict 3D Gaussians from sparse inputs in single forward pass, eliminating per-scene optimization and enabling fast, scalable 3D reconstruction. Despite their rapid inference, many existing feed-forward methods remain inefficient in their primitive allocation. Natural scenes exhibit substantial spatial variation in texture and geometric complexity, yet prior methods typically adopt rigid pixel-wise prediction paradigm, assigning one Chen et al. (2024c); Xu et al. (2024b); He et al. (2026) or multiple Charatan et al. (2024); Tang et al. (2024) Gaussians to every pixel. This uniform allocation forces the network to populate large, textureless regions with thousands of primitives. Consequently, the generated 3D representations can suffer from substantial spatial redundancy. This redundancy increases representation storage costs and motivates more compact 3D priors for downstream tasks. To address this issue, we introduce CompactSplat, novel feed-forward framework for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction with content-aware Gaussian allocation. Instead of retaining primitive at every pixel, CompactSplat allocates Gaussians according to image texture, using sparse primitives in homogeneous regions while concentrating denser predictions in areas with rich texture. To achieve this adaptive allocation, we decouple the primitive generation process into two complementary components. First, Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) analyzes the input views to estimate regional texture complexity and partition each image with quadtree. Second, Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) uses this guidance to sample explicit Gaussian attributes from pooled multiresolution attribute pyramid. Together, these components enable CompactSplat to adapt its primitive density to the input texture, reducing spatial redundancy while retaining strong reconstruction quality. Crucially, CompactSplat provides unified paradigm for controllable inference. Owing to the scaleaware synergy between TAP and HPS, our framework naturally supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time. By modulating single partition threshold, the model can select different trade-offs between rendering fidelity and primitive countwithout requiring any network retraining or auxiliary modules. This intrinsic adaptability provides an on-the-fly mechanism to select different representation sizes using single set of pretrained weights. Ultimately, CompactSplat establishes more compact paradigm for 3D representation. By replacing rigid pixel-wise allocation with texture-driven primitive allocation, our approach adapts to spatial variations in image content. In our experiments, it delivers high-fidelity reconstructions with fewer primitives. This allocation transforms dense, redundant outputs into compact 3D representations with tunable primitive count. In summary, our contributions are as follows: 2 We propose CompactSplat, feed-forward framework for compact sparse-view 3D reconstruction. By combining Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) with Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS), our method adaptively allocates 3D Gaussians based on image texture, significantly reducing spatial redundancy. We introduce controllable inference paradigm for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. With single partition threshold, CompactSplat supports dynamic, on-the-fly sparsity control. This capability enables seamless trade-offs between visual fidelity and primitive count using single set of network weights, completely eliminating the need for sparsity-specific retraining. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K and ACID demonstrate that CompactSplat achieves competitive quality with fewer primitives. It retains strong performance on both standard metrics and high-resolution rendering consistency, while cross-dataset evaluation on DTU, DL3DV, and ScanNet reveals qualitycompactness trade-offs.

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.content: 2.1 3D Gaussian Splatting Since the advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) Mildenhall et al. (2021), novel view synthesis has advanced rapidly, evolving from implicit MLPs to grid-based Müller et al. (2022); Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022) and anti-aliased Barron et al. (2021, 2022) representations. To further accelerate rendering, recent paradigms shifted towards explicit point-based architectures. Notably, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Kerbl et al. (2023) revolutionized the field by modeling scenes with semi-transparent, anisotropic ellipsoids, enabling photorealistic, real-time rendering via differentiable rasterization. Consequently, proliferation of extensions has emerged to refine 3DGS. These include optimizations for training stability Cheng et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024); Radl et al. (2024); Diolatzis et al. (2024), anti-aliasing techniques Yan et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2024); Song et al. (2024); Liang et al. (2024), and adaptations for dynamic scenes Luiten et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2023); Wan et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2023); He et al. (2024). Additionally, several works focus on compressing these representations to reduce storage and accelerate inference Girish et al. (2024); Navaneet et al. (2024); Niedermayr et al. (2024); Lee et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024b).

sections.title: 2.2 Generalizable 3D Reconstruction
sections.content: To bypass the computationally expensive per-scene optimization of traditional 3DGS, recent literature has explored feedforward models that directly predict Gaussian attributes from sparse inputs. Splatter Image Szymanowicz et al. (2024) pioneered the translation of 2D images into Gaussian parameter maps. Subsequent frameworks integrated geometric priors to enhance spatial understanding; for instance, pixelSplat Charatan et al. (2024) utilized epipolar geometry, while MVSplat Chen et al. (2024c) and DepthSplat Xu et al. (2024b) leveraged cost volumes and cross-task depth interactions. Further advancements addressed specific challenges, such as expanding synthesis ranges Wang et al. (2024b), improving geometric surfaces via 2DGS He et al. (2026), and handling unposed inputs Kang et al. (2025); Jiang et al. (2025). VGGT Wang et al. (2025) and MV-DUSt3R Tang et al. (2025) likewise reconstruct uncalibrated views, while CompactSplat assumes known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Other pipelines introduced triplane representations Zou et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2024a) and canonical space generation Ye et al. (2024) for feedforward 3D reconstruction and generation. SplatFormer Chen et al. (2024a) instead uses point transformer to refine an already optimized Gaussian scene for novel-view extrapolation. Pixel-wise prediction strategies, including multi-layered approaches like HiSplat Tang et al. (2024), can generate redundant primitives in homogeneous regions. Recent methods explore alternatives: TokenGS Ren et al. (2026) uses learnable queries to decouple Gaussian count from image resolution and view count, while C3G An et al. (2025) predicts compact Gaussian set from unposed multiview images using learned queries. VolSplat Wang et al. (2026) lifts features using predicted depth and decodes Gaussians from occupied voxels. Off The Grid Moreau et al. (2026) detects subpixel primitive positions and adapts patch density using image entropy. CompactSplat adopts contentaware allocation paradigm based on an image-space quadtree. TAP concentrates finer partitions in textured regions, while HPS samples pooled Gaussian attributes and modulates primitive scales according to block footprints. This spatial hierarchy supports inference-time qualitycompactness control with one checkpoint, reducing per-view redundancy while preserving detail at the selected operating point.

sections.title: 3.1 Model Architecture
sections.content: Figure 2: Overview of CompactSplat. dual-path encoder first extracts and fuses multi-view and single-view features from sparse inputs, which are then processed by multi-scale U-Net. Concurrently, the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) evaluates scene complexity based on userdefined threshold to generate multi-level spatial masks. Guided by these masks, the Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) adaptively extracts features across decoder levels. Ultimately, this paradigm allocates sparse samples (S.S.) from low-resolution (L.R.) maps to flat regions, and dense samples (D.S.) from high-resolution (H.R.) maps to texturally complex areas. Building upon the robust feature extraction paradigms established in recent feed-forward models He et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2024b), CompactSplat employs dual-path encoder to capture both multiview correspondences and single-view geometric priors. For the single-view branch, we utilize pretrained monocular depth backbone (e.g., Depth Anything V2 Yang et al. (2024)) to extract structural and semantic cues, which are particularly beneficial for ill-posed regions lacking cross-view overlaps. Concurrently, the multi-view branch processes the inputs through selfand cross-attention mechanisms Vaswani et al. (2017); Liu et al. (2021b) to construct plane-sweep cost volumes Chen et al. (2024c); Collins (1996), enforcing strict multi-view consistency. The complementary features from both branches are then concatenated to form unified volumetric representation. This fused feature volume is subsequently fed into multi-scale 2D U-Net Ronneberger et al. (2015) architecture. Unlike prior works that deterministically upsample all features into single, fullresolution map for pixel-wise Gaussian prediction, our architecture decouples primitive generation to eliminate spatial redundancy, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Specifically, we introduce the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP), which analyzes spatial frequency and regional complexity from the inputs to produce set of hierarchical partition masks. These masks dynamically dictate the appropriate Level of Detail (LoD) for representing different regions of the scene. Guided by the TAP masks, our Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) predicts explicit Gaussian attributesincluding 3D center, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonicsdirectly from the multi-scale intermediate features of the U-Net decoder. Crucially, large, homogeneous regions are assigned to lower-resolution feature levels, allowing single, scale-modulated Gaussian to seamlessly tile broad planar surfaces. In contrast, structurally complex areas are routed to the highest-resolution decoder features to preserve intricate geometric details. This multi-scale routing paradigm not only captures fine geometry but also naturally enables dynamic sparsity control, resulting in highly compact yet expressive 3D representation. The core motivation behind the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) is to replace redundant pixel-wise generation with adaptive, density-aware primitive allocation. To this end, we formulate the image partitioning as top-down quadtree decomposition driven by local textural complexity. This design is motivated by the inherent coupling of geometry and appearance within single 3D Gaussian primitive. In natural environments, geometric complexity (e.g., depth discontinuities, occlusions, and structural boundaries) almost inevitably manifests as high-frequency textural variance. Although the converse is not strictly trueintricate textures frequently lie on structurally flat surfacesrelying on textural complexity as subdivision proxy guarantees conservative and sufficient upper bound. It ensures that all complex geometries receive dense primitive allocation, while aggressively pruning homogeneous regions where neither geometry nor texture demands high-resolution modeling.

sections.title: 3.3 Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS)
sections.content: While the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) determines the optimal spatial layout and density of the primitives, the Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) maps these abstract spatial partitions into explicit 3D Gaussian attributes. To this end, HPS performs scale-conditioned sampling from foundational scene representation. However, directly sampling from this high-frequency field for large, homogeneous partitions would inherently lead to aliasing artifacts and mismatch in the receptive field. To address this, we construct discrete attribute scale space = {AL1, . . . , A1, A0}. Starting with the full-resolution field AL1 = Abase, each subsequent coarser level Al is derived by progressively applying spatial low-pass filter (e.g., local aggregation). This multi-scale representation ensures that features at lower Level of Detail (LoD) indices naturally encapsulate broader regional contexts, perfectly mirroring the TAP quadtree hierarchy. 6: % 2. The queried vector ak encapsulates base properties such as opacity, rotation, spherical harmonics, and relative scale multiplier sk. To guarantee that the allocated primitive physically spans its designated spatial partition, the final scale of the Gaussian, denoted as sk, is explicitly modulated by the quadtree node dimensions: sk = sk bk (3) This explicit scale conditioning elegantly bridges the gap between 2D partition logic and 3D geometry. It enables single Gaussian, sampled from deeper level of the scale space, to morphologically expand and seamlessly tile expansive planar surfaces. This fundamentally breaks the representational redundancy of rigid pixel-wise predictions while rigorously preserving the rendering quality of high-frequency intricate details. sections.title: 3.4 Training Strategy
sections.content: A core objective of CompactSplat is to establish unified paradigm for controllable inference, enabling dynamic trade-offs between rendering fidelity and sparsity without network retraining. To achieve this, the model must be exposed to varying partition thresholds τ during the training process. However, jointly optimizing for multi-view geometric consistency and dynamic primitive pruning from scratch introduces severe training instability. To mitigate this, we propose tailored two-stage curriculum learning strategy. Stage 1: Dense Geometric Initialization. In the initial phase, we strictly fix the partition threshold to τ = 0. Under this condition, the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) behaves conservatively, decomposing the feature maps at the highest Level of Detail (LoD) across the entire scene. This dense supervision isolates the learning objective, forcing the dual-path encoder and the multi-scale U-Net to focus exclusively on establishing robust multi-view correspondences and extracting accurate geometric priors, completely free from the confounding effects of adaptive sparsity. Stage 2: Sparsity-Aware Fine-Tuning. Once the network has converged to reliable geometric understanding, we introduce stochastic thresholding. In this subsequent stage, τ is randomly sampled from predefined uniform distribution τ U(0, τmax) at each training iteration. This strategy exposes the model to continuous spectrum of pruning ratios. Crucially, it forces the Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) to accurately learn the geometric scale multipliers for lower-resolution Gaussians, ensuring they can morphologically expand to seamlessly tile broad, homogeneous regions under aggressive pruning scenarios. Through this two-stage curriculum, single set of pretrained weights inherently acquires the versatility to reconstruct scenes at arbitrary sparsity levels on the fly.

sections.title: 3.5 Training Loss
sections.content: To optimize our feed-forward architecture, we apply direct photometric supervision between the synthesized views and the corresponding target images. The overall objective function is formulated as joint optimization of pixel-level fidelity and perceptual quality. Specifically, for training batch containing samples, the loss is defined as: Ltotal = (cid:88) m=1 (cid:0)MSE (cid:0)I render, gt (cid:1) + λ LPIPS (cid:0)I render, gt (cid:1)(cid:1) , (4) render and where gt denote the m-th rendered output and its corresponding ground truth, respectively. Consistent with established training protocols in recent generalizable 3DGS frameworks Charatan et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024c); Xu et al. (2024b); He et al. (2026), the scaling factor λ for the perceptual loss is empirically set to 0.05.

4 Experiment
4.1 Main Results
sections.content: Figure 3: Multi-resolution rendering comparison of 3D scenes. We visualize rendered RGB images and depth maps at three scaling factors: 1 (blue box), 2 (green box), and 4 (red box). Under higher magnification, structural deficiencies in conventional 3D representations become increasingly apparent. In the RGB domain, primitive sparsity causes unfilled gaps, manifesting as dark, hollow regions. Correspondingly, in the depth space (where yellow indicates near and blue indicates distant surfaces), these geometric discontinuities erroneously register as spurious near-field artifacts. In contrast, CompactSplats scale-modulated primitives seamlessly tile the surfaces, yielding watertight geometry and artifact-free renderings across all resolutions. Datasets.To comprehensively evaluate our approach, we benchmark CompactSplat across diverse set of environments commonly utilized in generalizable 3DGS literature. Specifically, we conduct experiments on RealEstate10K (RE10K) Zhou et al. (2018) for indoor scenes and ACID Liu et al. (2021a) for outdoor aerial trajectories, strictly adhering to the official train-test splits and precomputed camera poses established by prior works. To further validate the cross-dataset generalization and the robustness of our context-aware partitioning on complex geometries, we extend our evaluation to the DTU Jensen et al. (2014), DL3DV Ling et al. (2024), and the highly challenging ScanNet Dai et al. (2017) datasets. Comprehensive cross-dataset evaluations are detailed in the supplementary material. Baselines.Our framework is compared against leading sparse-view feedforward 3DGS models, including PixelSplat Charatan et al. (2024), MVSplat Chen et al. (2024c), TranSplat Zhang et al. (2025), HiSplat Tang et al. (2024), DepthSplat Xu et al. (2024b), SurfSplat He et al. (2026) and YonoSplat Ye et al. (2025). While architectures like PixelSplat and HiSplat indiscriminately predict multiple Gaussians per pixel, methods such as MVSplat, TranSplat, DepthSplat, SurfSplat and YonoSplat restrict their generation to single primitive per pixel. Because our core contribution lies in decisively breaking the 1:1 pixel-to-primitive barrier to eliminate spatial redundancy, benchmarking against this latter group establishes highly rigorous baseline for evaluating representational efficiency. Qualitative Comparisons. Visual inspections of the rendered novel views in Figure 3 demonstrate that CompactSplat achieves photorealistic quality that is highly competitive with, and frequently surpasses, current state-of-the-art feed-forward methods. This superiority becomes particularly evident under high-resolution magnification. While baseline models often struggle with spatial voids, noisy boundaries, and spurious artifacts due to their rigid primitive allocation, CompactSplat maintains strict structural integrity. By leveraging complexity-aware allocation, our method seamlessly tiles flat planar surfaces with scale-modulated primitives while accurately preserving high-frequency edges. Consequently, it yields strictly watertight geometries and visually coherent structures that remain exceptionally robust even upon close inspection. Additional qualitative comparisons across various scenes are provided in our supplementary video. Quantitative Results. The objective metrics presented in Table 1 and Table 2 further corroborate the transformative efficiency of our architecture. Across standard fidelity metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) and the structure-aware HRRC metric, CompactSplat consistently matches or exceeds the performance of leading baselines. Crucially, it achieves this high-fidelity synthesis while drastically reducing the total Number of Gaussians. By pioneering departure from the conventional pixel-wise prediction paradigm, CompactSplat establishes highly compact representation. Furthermore, this compactness is inherently controllable; our architecture allows users to dynamically modulate the pruning ratio on the fly, offering an unprecedented capability to balance rendering quality and memory footprint without requiring any network retraining.

sections.title: 4.2 Analysis of Dynamic Sparsity Control
sections.content: A core capability of CompactSplat is its inherent support for dynamic sparsity control without requiring network retraining. To investigate the efficacy of this mechanism, we systematically analyze the trade-off between reconstruction quality and representational compactness by modulating the partition threshold τ during inference, which effectively controls the average Gaussians Per Pixel. Figure 4: Quantitative analysis. By modulating the partition threshold τ at inference time, CompactSplat continuously traverses the Pareto frontier. The model achieves extreme reductions in primitive count (measured in Gaussian per pixel, GPP) with virtually negligible degradation in rendering fidelity. Quantitative Trade-offs. We evaluate our three model variants (Ours-S, Ours-B, and Ours-L) across continuous spectrum of GPP constraints (see Fig. 4). As demonstrated by the objective metrics, CompactSplat exhibits highly resilient Pareto frontier. Modulating the threshold to reduce the GPP within reasonable operational range incurs only marginal degradation in standard fidelity metrics. In exchange for this negligible drop in quantitative performance, our method yields substantial gains in representational compactness. This asymmetric trade-off confirms that the model successfully eliminates spatial redundancy, offering users highly flexible knob to drastically reduce memory footprint and rendering overhead while rigorously preserving overall scene integrity. Qualitative Observations. This robust quantitative performance is further corroborated by visual inspections of the rendered RGB, depth, and normal maps across varying GPP configurations (see Fig. 5). We observe distinct and highly complementary geometric behaviors at opposite ends of the sparsity spectrum. Operating at high GPP allows the network to allocate dense, highresolution primitives along intricate structures, yielding exceptionally sharp edges and crisp high-frequency boundaries. Conversely, operating at lower GPP forces the architecture to leverage larger, scalemodulated primitives sampled from deeper Figure 5: Qualitative analysis. Visualizations under pyramid levels. Interestingly, this highly varying GPP settings reveal an elegant architectural pruned setting is intrinsically suited for trade-off. Lower GPP limits enforce the use of exmodeling broad, homogeneous planar surpanded, scale-modulated primitives, yielding smoother, faces (e.g., walls and floors). By seamlessly watertight planar surfaces. Conversely, higher GPP tiling these expansive areas with single, exsettings allocate denser primitives to more faithfully panded Gaussians, the low-GPP configurarecover high-frequency edges and complex boundaries. tion fundamentally eliminates the spatial voids and "hollow" artifacts common in traditional sparse-view 3DGS, resulting in strictly watertight and visually coherent structural reconstructions. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we presented CompactSplat, novel feed-forward framework designed to overcome the severe spatial redundancy inherent in current sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting models. By synergizing Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) with Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS), our approach decisively breaks away from the rigid pixel-wise prediction paradigm, adaptively allocating primitives based on regional complexity. This scale-aware representation not only achieves stateof-the-art rendering fidelity across multiple datasets but also inherently supports dynamic sparsity control during inference. Consequently, CompactSplat delivers highly compact 3D priors, offering flexible, on-the-fly trade-offs between reconstruction quality and memory footprint.

sections.title: A Technical Appendices and Supplementary Material
sections.content: A.1 Preliminaries Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) frameworks bypass the computationally heavy perscene optimization by directly inferring 3D scene representation from sparse set of observations. Operating in single forward pass, these networks typically adopt dense, pixel-aligned prediction paradigm. Specifically, given source views {I v}V v=1 along with their corresponding camera intrinsics {kv}V v=1 and extrinsics {Tv}V v=1, standard feedforward model fθ outputs set of Gaussian primitives for every pixel coordinate: fθ : {(I v, kv, Tv)}V v=1 (cid:55) HW (cid:91) j=1 (cid:0)µv , αv , rv , sv , cv (cid:1) v=1 , (5) where and represent the spatial dimensions of the input images. The tuple defines the explicit attributes of the j-th Gaussian originating from view v: its 3D center coordinate µv , opacity αv , rotation quaternion rv , and spherical harmonics cv . , scaling factor sv The feasibility of this dense prediction relies heavily on the robust geometric priors extracted by modern vision backbones (e.g., ViTs Ranftl et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2024a); Fang et al. (2025); Gao et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025)). By unprojecting these rich 2D features into 3D space using camera parameters, the network establishes rigid pixel-to-Gaussian mapping that can be supervised end-to-end via differentiable rasterization. However, this rigid formulation indiscriminately populates the 3D space with primitives regardless of the underlying scene complexity. By forcing strict 1:1 mapping between pixels and Gaussians, existing architectures inevitably generate severe spatial redundancy in homogeneous regions and fail to exploit the geometric priors of piecewise planar surfaces. It is precisely this fundamental bottleneck in representational efficiency that CompactSplat seeks to overcome. A.2 Encoder Architecture We adopt dual-branch encoder design to extract both monocular and multi-view features for robust 3D reasoning, following the architecture proposed by DepthSplat Xu et al. (2024b) and subsequent SurfSPlat He et al. (2026). Multi-view Branch. The multi-view encoder begins with lightweight ResNet-style backbone composed of stride-2 convolutional layers, yielding spatially downsampled feature maps by factor of s. To enable view aggregation, we employ multi-view Swin Transformer Liu et al. (2021b) consisting of 6 stacked selfand cross-attention layers. This module outputs multi-view-aware features (cid:8)F i(cid:9)N We further adopt the plane-sweep stereo technique Collins (1996); Xu et al. (2023) to construct geometric consistency. We uniformly sample candidate depths between near and far bounds. Given reference view and source view j, we warp features Fj to view at each depth dm, resulting in (cid:110) i=1, where H . These warped volumes are compared to Fi via dot-product similarity to construct C. (cid:111)D ji dm m=1 cost volume Ci s D. Single-view Branch. We utilize the ViT backbone from Depth Anything V2 model Yang et al. (2024) to extract monocular features. The output has spatial resolution of 1/14 relative to the original image and is bilinearly upsampled to match the cost volume resolution, yielding monocular features Cm. H and Ci are concatenated U-Net and Depth Prediction. The monocular and multi-view features along the channel dimension and processed by 2D U-Net to produce depth candidates Di D. softmax operation is applied over the depth axis, followed by weighted summation to generate the predicted depth map. 14 To enhance depth quality, we employ hierarchical cascade structure Gu et al. (2020), refining the predicted depth to Di , which is subsequently upsampled to full resolution using DPT head Ranftl et al. (2021). ds 2H 2W Attribute Prediction. The predicted depth is used to reconstruct Gaussian positions. For estimating the remaining Gaussian attributessuch as scale multipliers, high-frequency SH coefficients, and opacitywe apply an additional DPT head, conditioned on concatenation of the input image, predicted depth, and encoder features. Hyperparameter Selection. The downsample scale is set to 4. Channel number is set to 128, channel number is set to 128. The channel number Cm of the monocular feature is set to 64 for small model, 96 for base model, 128 for large model. Gaussian Processor. The Surface Continuity Prior(SCP) and the Forced Alpha Blending methods from Surfsplat have been adopted to process the gaussian attributes. Note: Our implementation is consistent with DepthSplat Xu et al. (2024b) and SurfSplat He et al. (2026) for reproducibility. No architectural modifications are made to the encoder unless otherwise stated. A.3 Implementation Details. CompactSplat is implemented in PyTorch Paszke et al. (2019) and optimized using the AdamW optimizer Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) coupled with cosine annealing learning rate schedule. For the core components of our proposed architecture, we set the maximum block size in the TextureAware Partitioner to Smax = 16. During the sparsity-aware fine-tuning stage of our curriculum, the dynamic partition threshold is sampled uniformly up to τmax = 0.02. Following standard practices He et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2024b), we instantiate our model using varying capacities of the Depth Anything V2 Yang et al. (2024) monocular backbone (ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L), denoting these variants as Ours-S, Ours-B, and Ours-L, respectively. All models are trained on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Specifically, Ours-S is trained for 300K iterations with batch size of 16, whereas Ours-B and Ours-L are trained for 600K iterations with batch size of 8. The learning rate is configured at 2 106 for the pretrained monocular backbone and 2 104 for all newly initialized layers. Even when evaluated outside its primary training distribution, CompactSplat achieves rendering fidelity comparable to the state-of-the-art SurfSplat He et al. TokenGS and CompactSplat use two 256 256 inputs. C3G reports 224 224 training inputs and uses test-time target-camera alignment. Training and camera handling differ across methods. A.6 Extended Qualitative Results Figure 6 presents an additional set of reconstructed scenes across diverse environments. These qualitative visualizations further corroborate that CompactSplat reliably maintains photorealistic rendering quality and watertight geometric structures, all while empowering users with dynamic, on-the-fly control over representational compactness. Figure 6: More subjective comparison of generated 3D scenes. A.7 Limitations and Future Directions. While CompactSplat significantly improves representational efficiency, it leaves exciting room for future exploration. First, although our quadtree-based partitioning is highly efficient, it relies on rigid orthogonal grids. Exploring more sophisticated, shape-aware, or semantic-driven subdivision strategies could further push the boundaries of the Pareto frontier, extracting even higher visual fidelity at extreme pruning ratios. Second, our current formulation primarily eliminates spatial redundancy within individual views, leaving the inherent inter-view redundancy largely unexplored. Since multiple source cameras inevitably observe overlapping geometries, future research could investigate cross-view primitive pruning or multi-view fusion mechanisms to further condense the global 3D scene representation.
